query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short pre-oxidation heat treatment of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in a controlled low-partial-pressure oxygen atmosphere (~10^-6 atm O2) at approximately 900 °C for 2–4 hours will form an adherent oxide layer that significantly reduces subsequent oxidation and embrittlement during exposure to air at 800–1000 °C, relative to the untreated alloy, while preserving its room- and high-temperature tensile properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with 8–16% room-temperature ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.intervention: Apply a short pre-oxidation heat treatment under ~10^-6 atm O2 at 900 °C for 2–4 h
generation.conditions: After pre-oxidation, expose samples to air at 800–1000 °C for ≥5 h under strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, stable oxide scale formed on the alloy surface
generation.mechanism: The pre-oxidized, coherent oxide layer inhibits rapid oxygen ingress and prevents pesting by acting as a barrier, thereby preventing embrittlement and preserving mechanical strength at high temperatures
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized specimens will have substantially lower mass gain, less scale spallation, and minimal loss in tensile properties compared to untreated samples
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr suffers rapid oxidation, embrittlement, and mechanical degradation at 800–1000 °C in air
generation.boundary: Effective up to 1000 °C in air for at least 5 h of exposure at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1; scale performance under longer or cyclic exposures is unverified
generation.uncertainty: Exact scale formation kinetics and protective phase stability at higher temperatures or over prolonged times have not been fully characterized

falsification_experiment.design: Compare treated vs. untreated samples exposed to air at 900 °C and 1000 °C for 5 h under static or tensile conditions;
measurements: Mass change measurement for oxidation kinetics
SEM/EDS or XRD analysis of oxide scale morphology and composition
Tensile tests at 25 °C and 1000 °C to assess strength and ductility retention
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized alloy shows mass gains comparable to untreated specimens and exhibits similar or greater embrittlement after the same exposure conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Tetragonal and hexagonal Nb5Si3 and only hexagonal Nb5Si3 were present in the cast microstructures respectively of the alloys MG2 and MG7. Both these alloys exhibited severe macrosegregation of Si and Al, particularly the latter alloy that formed a “layered” microstructure. Both these alloys did not pest and formed alumina in their scales. At 1200 °C the former alloy suffered from internal oxidation and formed a “layered” scale in which the layer that was in contact with the substrate consisted of titanium oxide dispersed in alumina. The alloy MG7 formed a thin continuous well adhering alumina scale that was able to repair itself (self-heal) during oxidation []. The research presented in this paper is also aimed at extending further the study of alloys of the Nb-Ti-Si-Al-Hf quinary system with objective to “define” a compositional area (map) for alloys of the aforementioned system that can form continuous and self-healing αAl2O3 in isothermal oxidation in air. Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al. decision.trend: Over the past decade, several groups have investigated HfNbTaTiZr-based (and closely related) refractory high-entropy alloys by varying elements (Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr) or adding light interstitials like O/N. Early studies (PMC7514121 and PMC7514597) focused on mechanical properties and phase stability in as-cast HfNbTaTiZr or its partial-element variants, achieving promising strength–ductility balance at elevated temperatures. Later, others extended these concepts to doping with oxygen or nitrogen (PMC7299626) and to substituting or adding extra refractory elements (PMC10453588) to improve strength, ductility, or high-temperature formability. Despite significant progress in mechanical performance, oxidation resistance remains underexplored for the specific equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition. Prior demonstrations of pesting prevention in a non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy do not directly translate to the equiatomic alloy. Thus, a key gap persists: ensuring oxygen resistance in equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr at 800–1000 °C for multihour exposures without altering bulk composition or compromising mechanical properties.
decision.unsolved: Whether equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be rendered oxidation-resistant at high temperatures by means other than chemical doping is unknown. The formation and stability of a protective scale or interface that inhibits rapid oxygen ingress remains unproven for this specific composition, and a successful intervention must preserve both its notable ductility at room temperature and its high-temperature strength.
decision.lever: Apply a short pre-oxidation heat treatment in a controlled low-partial-pressure oxygen environment (e.g., ~10^-6 atm O2 for ~2–4 h at ~900 °C) to form and stabilize a dense, adherent oxide layer that prevents further oxidation up to 1000 °C in air for at least 5 h while preserving the alloy’s tensile properties at 1000 °C and room temperature. The hypothesis can be tested by exposing both treated and untreated samples to air at 800–1000 °C for multiple hours under tensile strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1, then verifying whether the pre-oxidized specimens exhibit a significantly reduced mass gain, less embrittlement, and minimal loss of high-temperature strength compared to untreated controls. A falsifying outcome would be catastrophic oxide spallation, a rapid mass increase, or severe embrittlement, indicating the pre-formed scale does not adequately protect the equiatomic alloy.
decision.why: This approach builds on findings that scale formation is critical to preventing “pesting” in related Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloys, while referencing the need for a method independent of bulk composition changes. Forming a stable oxide scale in a controlled environment is a known route to improving oxidation resistance of refractory alloys without sacrificing their intrinsic mechanical advantages.
